title: Right to Team Meetings
statement: You can ask for a child and family team meeting and take part in it.
source_says: To request additional child and family team meetings to address concerns
steps: Searched 'california.public.law WIC 16001.9', opened the public.law page, read paragraph (a)(39)(A)-(D). Also the cited paragraph number (39) matches the page.

title: Right to Team Meetings
statement: You should have one within 60 days of entering care and every six months after.
source_says: Within 60 days of entering foster care ... every six months thereafter ... at least every 90 days
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(39). (A) gives 60 days and every six months. (B) gives a shorter gap, at least every 90 days, for youth in a short-term residential therapeutic program or getting intensive home-based services, intensive case coordination, or therapeutic foster care. The entry leaves out the 90-day rule, so it is too low for those youth.
fix: You should have one within 60 days of entering care and every six months after. If you live in a short-term residential therapeutic program (STRTP) or get intensive services, you should have one at least every 90 days.

title: Right to Team Meetings
statement: You can ask for extra meetings about problems with your placement, visits, or services
source_says: placement disruption ... change in service needs ... addressing barriers to sibling or family visits ... addressing difficulties in coordinating services
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(39)(C) list of reasons for extra meetings.

title: Right to Team Meetings
statement: you can bring people who support you
source_says: To have both informal and formal support people participate, consistent with state law.
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(39)(D).

title: Right to Team Meetings
statement: You can ask for a meeting with your team and bring people you trust.
source_says: To request additional child and family team meetings ... To have both informal and formal support people participate
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(39)(C) and (D).

title: Right Not to Be Held in Juvenile Hall for Lack of a Home
statement: You cannot be kept in a juvenile detention facility just because you are in foster care or because there is no placement for you.
source_says: To not be detained in a juvenile detention facility ... the child welfare services department's inability to provide a foster care placement
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(8); joined three short quotes from that paragraph. Cited paragraph number (8) matches the page. Also cross-read the FindLaw copy of the section (current as of Jan 1, 2026), same content.

title: Right Not to Be Held in Juvenile Hall for Lack of a Home
statement: You cannot be put in juvenile hall just because there is nowhere else for you to stay.
source_says: the child welfare services department's inability to provide a foster care placement
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(8).

title: Right to Food, Clothing, and an Allowance
statement: You have the right to enough healthy food, clothes that fit, hygiene products, and an allowance that fits your age.
source_says: To receive adequate and healthy food, adequate clothing, grooming and hygiene products, and an age-appropriate allowance
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(3). Statute says 'adequate clothing'; it does not use the words 'that fit'. Cited paragraph number (3) matches.

title: Right to Food, Clothing, and an Allowance
statement: Your clothes and grooming should respect your culture and who you are.
source_says: shall respect the child's culture, ethnicity, and gender identity and expression.
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(3) second sentence.

title: Right to Food, Clothing, and an Allowance
statement: You get enough food, clothes, and things like soap and shampoo. You also get an allowance.
source_says: adequate clothing, grooming and hygiene products, and an age-appropriate allowance
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(3).

title: Right to a Free Credit Report
statement: From ages 14 to 17, you get a free credit report every year from each of the three credit agencies, and help fixing any mistakes on it.
source_name: WIC 16001.9(a)(32); CDSS Credit Reporting for Foster Youth page
source_says: For children 14 to 17 years of age, inclusive ... on an annual basis from each of the three major credit reporting agencies
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(32); paragraph number matches the citation. The statute paragraph does not use the word 'free'. Opened https://www.cdss.ca.gov/inforesources/cdss-programs/foster-care/credit-reporting-for-foster-youth, which says 'a free copy of any credit report pertaining to the youth annually'.

title: Right to a Free Credit Report
statement: Each year the county checks that no one has used your name for money. You get help fixing it.
source_name: WIC 16001.9(a)(32); CDSS Credit Reporting for Foster Youth page
source_says: Counties must request credit reports for foster youth 14 years of age or older
steps: Opened the CDSS credit reporting page and public.law 16001.9(a)(32) ('For children 14 to 17 years of age, inclusive'). The simple line drops the age. The right starts at 14, so a younger child reading this would be misled. The source also says the youth receives the report, not only that the county checks.
fix: From age 14 to 17, your worker gets your credit report each year and gives it to you. It shows if someone used your name for money. You get help fixing mistakes.

title: Right to a Free Credit Report
statement: Ask your social worker for your most recent credit report.
source_says: to receive a consumer credit report provided to the child by the social worker or probation officer on an annual basis
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(32): the report is given to the child by the social worker or probation officer.

title: Right to College and Career Information
statement: You have the right to information about school options, college and career paths, financial aid, and programs for current and former foster youth.
source_says: To have access to existing information regarding the educational options available ... information regarding financial aid for postsecondary education
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(28); paragraph number matches. Also read the FindLaw copy (current as of Jan 1, 2026), whose (28) covers career and postsecondary coursework, financial aid, and specialized programs at public universities and community colleges.

title: Right to College and Career Information
statement: You get to learn about college, jobs, and money to pay for school.
source_says: information regarding financial aid for postsecondary education
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(28).

title: Right to Work
statement: You have the right to work and build job skills at a level that fits your age.
source_says: To work and develop job skills at an age-appropriate level, consistent with state law.
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(31); paragraph number matches the citation.

title: Right to Work
statement: You can have a job.
source_says: To work and develop job skills at an age-appropriate level, consistent with state law.
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(31). The simple line drops 'age-appropriate' and 'consistent with state law'. The right depends on the youth's age and state work rules.
fix: You can have a job when you are old enough under state law.

title: Right to See Your Records
statement: You can see your court file
source_says: to view and receive a copy of the court file, subject to existing federal and state confidentiality laws
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(34)(A).

title: Right to See Your Records
statement: you can view and get copies of your child welfare, court, and school records at no cost until you are 26
source_says: at no cost to the child until the child is 26 years of age ... subject to existing federal and state confidentiality laws
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(36). Records, no cost and age 26 all match. The entry leaves out 'subject to existing federal and state confidentiality laws', so some parts may be held back.
fix: You can see your court file. You can view and get free copies of your child welfare, court, and school records until you are 26. Privacy laws may keep some parts from you.

title: Right to See Your Records
statement: Your juvenile court records are kept confidential from others.
source_says: To the confidentiality of all juvenile court records consistent with existing law.
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(35). Citation (a)(34)-(36) matches the three paragraphs.

title: Right to See Your Records
statement: You can see your own files and get free copies.
source_says: at no cost to the child until the child is 26 years of age
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(36). The simple line drops the age 26 cutoff for free copies and the confidentiality limit.
fix: You can see your own files. Copies are free until you turn 26. Some parts may be kept private by law.

title: Right to Go to Independent Living Program Classes
statement: You have the right to attend Independent Living Program classes and activities.
source_says: To attend Independent Living Program classes and activities ... meets the age requirements
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(29) twice. The paragraph gives the right only if the child 'meets the age requirements'. The paragraph does not say what the ages are. The entry leaves the age condition out.
fix: If you are old enough for the Independent Living Program, you have the right to go to its classes and activities. Ask your social worker what age it starts in your county.

title: Right to Go to Independent Living Program Classes
statement: No one can keep you from them as a punishment.
source_says: and to not be prevented by caregivers from attending as a consequence or punishment.
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(29). The statute names caregivers; the entry says 'no one'.

title: Right to Go to Independent Living Program Classes
statement: You can go to classes that teach adult life skills. No one can take them away to punish you.
source_says: meets the age requirements
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(29). Same age condition is missing from the simple line.
fix: When you are old enough, you can go to classes that teach adult life skills. Your caregiver cannot take them away to punish you.

title: Right to Paperwork in Your Language
statement: You have the right to get court reports, your case plan, your transition plan, and a copy of your rights in the language you speak best.
source_says: those items shall be provided in the child's primary language ... to be provided a copy of the child's rights in the child's primary language
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(34)(B) and (a)(40)(B). Per the page, 'those items' in (34)(B) are the court report, case plan, and transition to independent living plan (TILP), where the child is entitled to receive them. (40)(B) applies when the child's primary language is not English. Both cited paragraphs match.

title: Right to Paperwork in Your Language
statement: You get your papers in your own language.
source_says: those items shall be provided in the child's primary language
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(34)(B). 'Papers' here means the court report, case plan, TILP, and the copy of rights, not every paper.

title: Right to Report Problems
statement: You can report mistreatment without fear.
source_says: contact any or all of these offices immediately upon request regarding violations of rights ... to be free from threats or punishment for making complaints
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(41). The entry cites (a) in general; the exact paragraph is (a)(41).

title: Right to Report Problems
statement: You can tell someone when you are treated badly. You will not get in trouble.
source_says: to be free from threats or punishment for making complaints
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(41).

title: Right to Report Problems
statement: Foster Care Ombudsperson: 1-877-846-1602 or fosteryouthhelp.ca.gov
source_name: Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson, File a Complaint page
steps: Searched 'Foster Care Ombudsperson phone', opened fosteryouthhelp.ca.gov/file-a-complaint/, read the toll-free number. The CDSS county complaints page lists the same number as 1-(877) 846-1602. The site address is the page I opened.

title: Right to Healthcare
statement: You have the right to medical, dental, and mental health care.
source_says: To access and receive medical, dental, vision, mental health, and substance use disorder services
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(22)(A).

title: Right to Healthcare
statement: This includes the right to understand and agree to your own treatment, especially as you get older.
source_says: At 12 years of age or older, to consent to or decline health care services to prevent, test for, or treat sexually transmitted diseases
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9. (22) gives the right 'to have diagnoses and services explained in an understandable manner'. The consent rights are narrower than 'your own treatment': (24)(B) covers contraception and pregnancy care at any age; (24)(C) covers STD, HIV and mental health services at 12 or older. The section does not give a general right to agree to all treatment.
fix: You have the right to have your care explained in a way you understand. At 12 or older, you can say yes or no on your own to some kinds of care, like mental health care and testing or treatment for STDs.

title: Right to Healthcare
statement: You get to see a doctor, a dentist, and a counselor. As you get older, you get more say in your own care.
source_says: To access and receive medical, dental, vision, mental health, and substance use disorder services ... At 12 years of age or older, to choose, whenever feasible
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(22)(A), (24)(C) and (25).

title: Right to Healthcare
statement: You can choose your own doctor and therapist when possible.
source_says: At 12 years of age or older, to choose, whenever feasible ... if payment for the service is authorized under applicable federal Medicaid law or other approved insurance
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(25). The right to choose a provider starts at age 12 and applies only if Medi-Cal or other approved insurance pays for the service. The tip leaves out both conditions.
fix: If you are 12 or older, you can choose your own doctor or therapist when that is possible and your insurance, like Medi-Cal, covers them.

title: Right to Healthcare
statement: As a teen, you have more privacy with your health decisions.
source_says: At 12 years of age or older, to consent to or decline health care services
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(24)(C); per the page this applies to STD, HIV and mental health services, without the consent or knowledge of any adult. The age in the statute is 12, not 13.

title: Right to Normal Childhood Activities
statement: You have the right to participate in normal activities like sports, school clubs, sleepovers, field trips, and after-school programs.
source_says: Every child adjudged a dependent child of the juvenile court shall be entitled to participate in age-appropriate extracurricular, enrichment, and social activities.
steps: Searched 'WIC 362.05 age-appropriate extracurricular', opened the FindLaw page (current as of Jan 1, 2026), read (a)(1). The statute does not name sports, clubs, sleepovers or field trips; it uses the general words quoted. Also read public.law 16001.9(a)(16): 'To participate in extracurricular, cultural, racial, ethnic, personal enrichment, and social activities'.

title: Right to Normal Childhood Activities
statement: Your foster parent can approve these activities using the "Reasonable and Prudent Parent Standard" — they do not need to ask the social worker for permission for normal kid stuff.
source_says: make careful and sensible parental decisions, without prior approval from the case social worker
steps: Opened FindLaw 362.05(a)(1): caregivers 'shall use a reasonable and prudent parent standard in determining whether to give permission'. Opened the CDSS Caregiver FAQs page for the words on no prior approval from the social worker.

title: Right to Normal Childhood Activities
statement: You get to do normal kid stuff, like sports, clubs, and sleepovers. Your foster parent can say yes.
source_says: shall use a reasonable and prudent parent standard in determining whether to give permission
steps: Opened FindLaw 362.05, read (a)(1). The caregiver decides, so the caregiver can also say no when a sensible parent would.

title: Right to Normal Childhood Activities
statement: You should not be treated differently from other kids.
source_says: A state or local regulation or policy shall not prevent, or create barriers to, participation in those activities.
steps: Opened FindLaw 362.05, read (a)(1).

title: Follow Reasonable Rules
statement: While you have rights, you are also expected to follow reasonable rules at your placement, like curfews and household expectations.
source_name: WIC 16001.9; Foster Youth Rights Handbook (Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson)
source_says: can have reasonable rules for when you use or don't use your cell phone.
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16001.9 (the cited law) and asked for any words on rules, curfew, duties or responsibilities: none, the section lists rights only. Opened the Foster Youth Rights Handbook: no sentence says a youth must follow house rules and curfew is not covered. It only says a caregiver can have reasonable rules for cell phone use (p. 16) and reasonable limits on computer use (p. 10). No source found for a stated duty or for curfews.
fix: Your caregiver can set fair house rules. Rules cannot take away your rights. If a rule feels unfair, talk to your social worker.

title: Follow Reasonable Rules
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16001.9 and checked for any duty on the child to follow rules, obey a curfew, or other responsibilities. Not on the page. The section is a list of rights, so it does not support an entry filed as a duty.
fix: Say that WIC 16001.9 lists your rights, and that house rules cannot take those rights away. Do not cite it as the source of a duty.

title: Follow Reasonable Rules
statement: If a rule violates your rights, you can challenge it through proper channels.
source_says: contact any or all of these offices immediately upon request regarding violations of rights
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(41): the offices are Community Care Licensing, the tribal authority where it applies, and the State Foster Care Ombudsperson. The tip does not name them.

title: Help the Child Maintain Family Connections
statement: The child has a right to maintain relationships with their parents, siblings, and other family members (unless the court says otherwise).
source_says: visit and contact siblings, family members, and relatives privately ... unless prohibited by court order
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(12).

title: Help the Child Maintain Family Connections
statement: As a caregiver, you should support these connections. This means helping with phone calls, facilitating visits, and speaking positively (or at least neutrally) about the child's family.
source_name: CDSS Caregiver Advocacy Network, Visitation page
source_says: Encourage the child's relationships with his parents and relatives. ... Cooperate in visiting arrangements between child and parents; and between child and siblings.
steps: Searched cdss.ca.gov for caregiver responsibilities on family visits, opened the CDSS Visitation page. It also says 'Cooperate in any telephone contacts between the child and the child's parents or other family members.' The page ties these to the placement agreement.

title: Help the Child Maintain Family Connections
statement: Help the child keep in touch with their family. Help with calls and visits, and speak kindly about their family.
source_name: CDSS Caregiver Advocacy Network, Visitation page
source_says: Cooperate in any telephone contacts between the child and the child's parents or other family members.
steps: Opened the CDSS Visitation page and read the caregiver responsibilities list.

title: Help the Child Maintain Family Connections
statement: do not stop visits on your own — only the court can do that.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, What to do if your child is removed; WIC 362.1
source_says: You can continue to visit with your child, unless the court finds that it is harming the child.
steps: Opened the self-help parents guide. Also opened public.law WIC 362.1: visitation is set in the court's order, and for sibling visits 'the court shall make a renewed finding' to keep a suspension. The CDSS Visitation page does not address a caregiver cancelling visits.

title: Help the Child Maintain Family Connections
statement: WIC §16002 – Sibling contact rights. WIC §362.1 – Visitation support. Caregiver responsibilities include supporting family connections.
source_says: to provide for ongoing and frequent interaction among siblings
steps: Opened public.law 16002 and 362.1. Both are real and are about sibling contact and visitation. But 16002 puts its duties on the responsible local agency, the social worker and the court, and 362.1 has no words about caregivers. Neither one puts a duty on caregivers. The caregiver duty is on the CDSS Visitation page (placement agreement).
fix: WIC 16002 (sibling contact) and WIC 362.1 (visits) put the duty on the county and the court. The caregiver's part comes from the foster care placement agreement. See the CDSS Caregiver Visitation page.

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: You have the right to go to your court hearings and see what is happening in your case.
source_says: A minor or nonminor dependent who is the subject of a juvenile court hearing ... is entitled to be present at the hearing.
steps: Searched 'WIC 349 minor entitled to be present', opened the Justia 2025 code page, read subdivision (a).

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: If you are 10 or older, the court should ask whether you were told about the hearing and whether you want to attend.
source_says: whether the minor or nonminor dependent was properly notified ... whether the minor or nonminor dependent was given an opportunity to attend
steps: Opened Justia WIC 349, read (d). This check happens when a youth 10 or older is not at the hearing. The statute asks whether the youth was 'given an opportunity to attend'; if the youth wished to come and had no chance, the court must continue the hearing unless that is not in the minor's best interest. The self-help children's guide also says a youth 10 or older must be told the court date.

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: You can also write a letter to the judge if you cannot be there or do not want to speak out loud.
source_says: Talk to the judge at a hearing or write the judge a letter, or
steps: WIC 349 and the self-help children's guide do not mention a letter. Opened the Foster Youth Rights Handbook from the Office of the Foster Care Ombudsperson (found by search) and read p. 57.

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: No one should prevent you from attending your hearings if you want to go.
source_says: Nothing in this section shall prevent or limit any minor's or nonminor dependent's right to attend
steps: Opened Justia WIC 349, read (e).

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: You can go to your court hearings. You can also write the judge a letter.
source_name: WIC 349(a); Foster Youth Rights Handbook p. 57
source_says: is entitled to be present at the hearing.
steps: Opened Justia WIC 349(a) and the Foster Youth Rights Handbook p. 57 ('write the judge a letter').

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: If you are nervous, you can bring a support person.
source_says: You have the right to ask for certain people to attend your court hearing.
steps: WIC 349 says nothing about a support person. Opened the Foster Youth Rights Handbook, read p. 34 (p. 55 says the youth can request the presence of interested persons). The source gives a right to ask, not a right to bring someone.
fix: If you are nervous, you can ask for a support person to come to court with you.

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: You do not have to speak if you do not want to — your attorney can speak for you.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide for children and youth; WIC 349(c)
source_says: Your lawyer is your advocate. They speak for you and fight for you in court.
steps: Opened the self-help children's guide (reached by redirect from the courts.ca.gov youth page that search returned). WIC 349(c) lets the youth address the court 'if they so desire'.

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: If you want to talk to the judge directly, ask your attorney to arrange it.
source_says: they have the right to address the court and participate in the hearing.
steps: Opened Justia WIC 349, read (c). public.law 16001.9(a)(34)(A) also lists 'to speak to the judge'.

title: Right to Attend Court
statement: WIC §349 – Child has the right to be present at hearings. Court must consider child's wishes.
source_says: they have the right to address the court and participate in the hearing.
steps: Opened Justia WIC 349 and read (a) to (e). The right to be present is there. The section does not say the court must consider the child's wishes when deciding the case. It deals with the child's wish to attend and to speak.
fix: WIC 349: You have the right to be at your hearings and to speak to the judge.

title: You Can Keep Working on Services After They End
statement: If the judge ends the county's reunification services, that is not the same as ending your parental rights.
source_name: Judicial Council, The Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 13
source_says: Termination of services is NOT the same as termination of parental rights.
steps: Searched for the booklet on courts.ca.gov, opened the PDF, read p. 13. (The PDF text runs two words together, 'astermination'; spacing fixed in the quote.)

title: You Can Keep Working on Services After They End
statement: You can keep doing classes, treatment, and counseling on your own
source_name: Judicial Council, The Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 13
source_says: You can continue with the services you want to try to take care of the problems
steps: Opened the booklet PDF, read p. 13.

title: You Can Keep Working on Services After They End
statement: your lawyer can ask the judge to change the order if things have changed.
source_says: upon grounds of change of circumstance or new evidence ... to change, modify, or set aside any order of court previously made
steps: Searched public.law for WIC 388, opened the page, read (a)(1). Under (d) the court orders a hearing if the child's best interests may be promoted. The booklet p. 33 describes the same paper. The citation matches.

title: You Can Keep Working on Services After They End
statement: If the county's help stops, you can keep going on your own.
source_name: Judicial Council, The Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 13
source_says: You can continue with the services you want to try to take care of the problems
steps: Opened the booklet PDF, read p. 13.

title: Right to the Least Restrictive Placement
statement: You should live in the most family-like setting that can meet your needs.
source_says: To be placed in the least restrictive setting possible ... unless a court orders otherwise.
steps: Opened public.law 16001.9, read (a)(4); paragraph number matches. The words 'family-like' are not in 16001.9. Opened public.law WIC 16000(a): 'to live in the least restrictive family setting promoting normal childhood experiences'.

title: Right to the Least Restrictive Placement
statement: A group setting should be used only when a family home cannot keep you safe or meet your needs.
source_says: Determine whether the needs of the child or nonminor dependent can be met through placement in a family-based setting
steps: This sentence is not in the cited (a)(4). Opened public.law WIC 16501.1(d): placement priority puts group care last, and for a short-term residential therapeutic program 'the case plan shall indicate the needs' that require it. Opened public.law WIC 361.22(e)(2): the court reviewing such a placement must decide whether a family-based setting can meet the child's needs.

title: Right to the Least Restrictive Placement
statement: You should live in a home with a family whenever that is possible.
source_says: to live in the least restrictive family setting promoting normal childhood experiences
steps: Opened public.law WIC 16000, read (a).

title: Right to College and Career Information
statement: Ask about the Chafee Grant and your college's foster youth program.
source_says: California Chafee Grant Program
steps: Searched csac.ca.gov for the Chafee Grant; the csac.ca.gov/chafee page would not load (client error). Opened the Foster Youth Rights Handbook, which lists the program by name on p. 31 with the chafee.csac.ca.gov address. Only the program's existence was checked; the tip states no amount or rule.

title: Right to Work
statement: Your social worker can help you get the papers you need to work.
source_says: Your school and your social worker/probation officer can help you get a work permit.
steps: WIC 16001.9 has no words on work papers. Opened the Foster Youth Rights Handbook, read p. 32, which also says 'You can have a job beginning at age 14, if you get a work permit.' (PDF text shows 'ofcer'; spelling fixed in the quote.)

title: Right to File a Grievance
statement: If you believe the social worker or agency is treating you unfairly, not following the law, or not providing required services, you can file a formal grievance.
source_name: CDSS MPP Division 31 section 31-020; CDSS Complaints About County Child Welfare Services Agencies page
steps: Searched cdss.ca.gov for MPP 31-020. The Division 31 PDF (cdss.ca.gov/Portals/9/Regs/cws1.pdf) was blocked by the site (robots_disallowed) and a second CDSS path failed (client error), so I could not read what 31-020 covers or who may use it. Opened the CDSS county complaints page instead: it says social worker conduct complaints 'should be addressed to the Director of the county CWS agency for resolution' and does not mention a formal grievance or section 31-020. The search budget for this run then ran out.
fix: If the county treats you unfairly, you can send a complaint to the Director of your county child welfare agency. Ask the county how its grievance process works and what it covers.

title: Right to File a Grievance
statement: You can also report concerns to the court through your attorney. If your rights are being violated, your attorney can file motions to address the problem.
source_says: Any parent or other person having an interest in a child who is a dependent child of the juvenile court
steps: Opened public.law WIC 388(a)(1): a parent may petition 'to change, modify, or set aside any order of court previously made' on changed circumstances or new evidence. Opened FindLaw WIC 317(d): counsel represents the parent 'at the detention hearing and at all subsequent proceedings before the juvenile court'. The booklet p. 23 says to call your lawyer as soon as possible if you disagree with the court report.

title: Right to File a Grievance
statement: If the county treats you unfairly, you can file a complaint. Your lawyer can also tell the judge.
source_name: CDSS Complaints About County Child Welfare Services Agencies page
source_says: should be addressed to the Director of the county CWS agency for resolution
steps: Opened the CDSS county complaints page (found by search). It sends complaints about social worker conduct to the county child welfare Director.

title: Right to File a Grievance
statement: If your social worker is not returning calls, note every attempt you make to contact them.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, What to do if your child is removed
source_says: If your social worker isn't returning your calls, locate the main number ... ask for a supervisor
steps: Opened the self-help parents guide. It covers the same problem and adds a step the tip leaves out: call the main number and ask for a supervisor.

title: Right to File a Grievance
statement: CDSS Manual of Policies and Procedures §31-020 (county grievance procedures)
steps: Searched cdss.ca.gov; the search returned the Division 31 manual PDF. The fetch was refused (robots_disallowed) and an alternate CDSS path gave a client error. I could not read 31-020, so I could not check whether it covers the unfair treatment, law, and services complaints the entry lists or only narrower issues.
fix: Have a person open MPP 31-020 and confirm what kinds of complaints it covers before keeping this citation.

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: If you cannot afford a lawyer, the juvenile court must appoint one for you.
source_name: WIC 317(a)(1), (b); Judicial Council booklet p. 3; Self-Help Guide for parents; Judicial Council hearing outline
steps: Two kinds of sources differ. The statute (FindLaw WIC 317, current as of Jan 1, 2026): (b) says 'the court shall appoint counsel for the parent or guardian' when the parent 'is presently financially unable to afford' one AND 'the child has been placed in out-of-home care' or the agency 'is recommending that the child be placed in out-of-home care', unless the parent waives; (a)(1) says otherwise 'the court may appoint counsel'. The court guides state it with no condition: booklet p. 3 'the judge will give you one if you cannot afford to hire your own'; self-help guide 'If you cannot afford a lawyer, the judge will assign one to you'; Judicial Council outline 'The court must appoint counsel for indigent parents at their first appearance'. Under the run rules, differing sources get COULD_NOT_VERIFY. The statute text is the narrower one.
fix: If you cannot pay for a lawyer and your child has been removed, or the county wants to remove your child, the court must give you a lawyer. In other cases the court may give you one. Ask the judge for a lawyer at your first hearing.

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: The court may ask later whether you can pay back some of the cost, based on what you can afford.
source_says: shall also be liable for any cost to the county or the court
steps: Opened FindLaw WIC 903.1 (current as of Jan 1, 2026): (a)(2) makes the parent liable for the cost of an attorney appointed for the parent in a dependency proceeding; (b) no liability if the petition 'is dismissed at or before the jurisdictional hearing'. Opened FindLaw WIC 903.47: 'Adopt a statewide standard for determining the ability to pay reimbursements for counsel'. The entry's own citation (WIC 317) does not cover repayment.

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: This happens at your very first hearing (the detention hearing).
source_says: at the detention hearing and at all subsequent proceedings before the juvenile court
steps: Opened FindLaw WIC 317, read (d). The Judicial Council hearing outline (courts.ca.gov btb_23_precon_juvenile_4.pdf) also says counsel is appointed 'at their first appearance'.

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: You have the right to talk to your lawyer privately before any hearing.
source_name: WIC 317; Judicial Council, The Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 23
source_says: You should always talk with your attorney before every court date, anyway.
steps: Opened FindLaw WIC 317 (the cited law): no words on a parent's right to meet privately with counsel before a hearing. Opened the booklet: p. 23 says the parent should talk with the attorney before every court date; it does not call this a right and does not say the talk is private. No source found that states this as a right.
fix: You should talk with your lawyer before every hearing. Ask your lawyer for a time to talk.

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: If you feel your attorney is not doing a good job, you can ask the judge for a new one
source_says: unless relieved by the court upon the substitution of other counsel or for cause
steps: Opened FindLaw WIC 317, read (d): the court can relieve appointed counsel when other counsel is substituted or for cause. The statute does not promise the judge will agree.

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: (this is called a "Marsden motion")
steps: WIC 317, the booklet and the self-help guide do not use the word Marsden. A courts.ca.gov search returned only appellate opinions; the one I opened (People v. Carter, C094949) was not a dependency case. The Judicial Council hearing outline does not cover it. The search budget for this run ran out before I could find a dependency source for this name.
fix: If you think your court-appointed lawyer is not doing a good job, you can ask the judge for a new one. (Keep the Marsden name only after a person checks a source.)

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: You get a lawyer even if you cannot pay. Your lawyer is on your side.
source_name: WIC 317(a)(1), (b); Judicial Council booklet p. 3; Self-Help Guide for parents
steps: Same split as the description. WIC 317(b) requires appointment when the parent cannot pay and the child is in, or the agency recommends, out-of-home care; (a)(1) says 'may appoint' otherwise. The booklet and self-help guide say it with no condition. Differing sources, so COULD_NOT_VERIFY under the run rules.
fix: If you cannot pay and your child was removed or may be removed, the court must give you a lawyer. Your lawyer is on your side.

title: Right to an Attorney
statement: WIC §317 – Court shall appoint counsel for indigent parents. See also Marsden motion procedure.
source_says: the child has been placed in out-of-home care ... the petitioning agency is recommending that the child be placed in out-of-home care
steps: Opened FindLaw WIC 317. The 'shall appoint' rule in (b) carries the out-of-home care condition; (a)(1) is 'may appoint'. The section says nothing about Marsden.
fix: WIC 317(b): the court must appoint a lawyer for a parent who cannot pay when the child is placed out of the home or the county is asking for that. WIC 317(a): in other cases the court may appoint one.

title: Right to Contest Allegations
statement: You have the right to deny the allegations in the petition and demand a trial (called a jurisdictional hearing).
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.684(a); rule 5.682
source_says: If the parent or guardian denies the allegations of the petition, the court must hold a contested hearing
steps: Searched courts.ca.gov for rules 5.682 and 5.684, opened both. Rule 5.682(a)(1) lists 'The right to a hearing by the court on the issues raised by the petition'. Naming note: the rule and the booklet (p. 29) call the trial a 'contested hearing'; it is the contested form of the jurisdiction hearing.

title: Right to Contest Allegations
statement: At trial, the agency must prove the allegations by a "preponderance of the evidence" — meaning they must show it is more likely than not that the allegations are true.
source_name: WIC 355(a); Judicial Council juvenile hearing outline (courts.ca.gov)
source_says: The Agency bears the burden to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the allegations in the petition are true
steps: Opened public.law WIC 355(a): 'Proof by a preponderance of evidence must be adduced'. Neither 355 nor rule 5.684 names who carries the burden, so opened the Judicial Council outline that search returned, which states it and cites WIC 355(a). I read the first 100,000 characters of that PDF. The 'more likely than not' gloss is the entry's own wording and was not on the pages.

title: Right to Contest Allegations
statement: You do not have to prove your innocence.
source_name: Judicial Council juvenile hearing outline, citing WIC 355(a)
source_says: The Agency bears the burden to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the allegations in the petition are true
steps: Opened the Judicial Council outline on courts.ca.gov. The burden is on the agency. I did not check WIC 355.1, which was not cited by the entry.

title: Right to Contest Allegations
statement: Your attorney can challenge the social worker's testimony, present counter-evidence, and argue that the case should be dismissed.
source_says: The preparer of the social study shall be made available for cross-examination upon a timely request by a party.
steps: Opened public.law WIC 355(b)(2). Rule 5.682 lists the rights 'to confront and to cross-examine adverse witnesses' and to compel witnesses. Rule 5.684(g): if not proved, 'the court must dismiss the petition and terminate any detention orders relating to the petition'.

title: Right to Contest Allegations
statement: You can say the county is wrong and ask for a trial. The county has to prove it. You do not have to prove you are innocent.
source_name: Rule 5.684(a); Judicial Council juvenile hearing outline citing WIC 355(a)
source_says: If the parent or guardian denies the allegations of the petition, the court must hold a contested hearing
steps: Opened rule 5.684 and the Judicial Council outline ('The Agency bears the burden to prove by a preponderance of the evidence').

title: Right to Contest Allegations
statement: Sometimes admitting certain things and focusing on getting services is faster.
source_says: The parent or guardian may elect to admit the allegations of the petition ... or plead no contest and waive further jurisdictional hearing
steps: Opened rule 5.682, read (d): the parent may admit, plead no contest, or submit. Only the option to admit was checked; 'faster' is advice and was not on the page.

title: Right to Contest Allegations
statement: WIC §355 – Jurisdictional hearing procedures. Agency bears the burden of proof by preponderance of evidence. See also WIC §334.
source_says: Proof by a preponderance of evidence must be adduced
steps: Opened public.law WIC 355(a). The section sets the standard; it does not itself name who carries the burden (the Judicial Council outline does, citing 355(a)). Opened public.law WIC 334: it only sets hearing dates ('within 30 days'; 'within 15 judicial days' if the minor is detained) and says nothing on proof.

title: Provide Relative Contact Information
statement: Give the social worker names and contact information for any relatives — grandparents, aunts, uncles, adult siblings, cousins, or close family friends.
source_name: Judicial Council, The Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 10 and p. 22; WIC 319(h)(3)
source_says: Bring to court the names and contact information of any relatives you think could possibly take care of your child
steps: Opened the booklet PDF, read p. 10 and p. 22 ('Let the social worker and your attorney know right away about any relatives'). Opened public.law WIC 319, which in (h)(3) refers to disclosure of 'the names, residences, and any known identifying information of any maternal or paternal relatives'. The self-help guide adds 'close connections'.

title: Provide Relative Contact Information
statement: California law requires the agency to consider relatives first for placement.
source_says: the relative seeking placement shall be the first placement to be considered and investigated.
steps: Searched public.law for WIC 361.3, opened it, read (a) ('preferential consideration shall be given to a request by a relative of the child for placement') and (c)(1). Per the page, family friends who are not related are not 'relatives' for this preference; WIC 16501.1(d)(1) separately lists relatives and nonrelative extended family members first in placement priority.

title: Provide Relative Contact Information
statement: Give your social worker the names and numbers of family who could care for your child. Do it early.
source_name: Judicial Council, The Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 22
source_says: Let the social worker and your attorney know right away about any relatives
steps: Opened the booklet PDF, read p. 22. (PDF text runs words together; spacing fixed in the quote.)

title: Provide Relative Contact Information
statement: WIC §309(e), §361.3 – Agency must identify and notify relatives. Relatives have preferential consideration for placement.
source_says: the social worker shall conduct, within 30 days, an investigation in order to identify and locate all grandparents
steps: Searched public.law for WIC 309, opened it, read (e): investigation within 30 days and written notice to located adult relatives. Opened public.law 361.3(a) for preferential consideration. Both citations match.

title: Right to Ask a Judge to Rehear a Referee's Decision
statement: If a referee, not a judge, decided something in your case, you can ask a judge to hear it again.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.542(a); WIC 252
source_says: a referee not acting as a temporary judge ... may be made by the child, parent, or guardian
steps: Searched courts.ca.gov for rule 5.542, opened it, read (a) and (c). Rehearing applies only when the referee was 'not acting as a temporary judge'. The entry leaves that out. Also the judge 'may, after reading the transcript of the proceedings, grant or deny the application'. Opened public.law WIC 252 for the same right.
fix: If a referee decided something in your case, and the referee was not sitting as a temporary judge, you can ask a judge to hear it again. The judge can say yes or no.

title: Right to Ask a Judge to Rehear a Referee's Decision
statement: You have 10 days from when you are served with the referee's written order.
source_says: At any time prior to the expiration of 10 days after service of a written copy of the order and findings of a referee
steps: Searched for WIC 252, opened public.law, read the first sentence. Rule 5.542(a) says 'before the expiration of 10 calendar days after service of a copy of the order and findings'. Both citations match.

title: Right to Ask a Judge to Rehear a Referee's Decision
statement: If a referee decided, you can ask a judge to look again. You only have 10 days.
source_says: a referee not acting as a temporary judge
steps: Opened rule 5.542(a). The 10 days is right (10 calendar days after service of the order and findings). The simple line drops the temporary judge condition and does not say the 10 days start at service.
fix: If a referee who was not sitting as a temporary judge decided, you can ask a judge to look again. You only have 10 days after you get the written order.

title: Visit Your Child Consistently
statement: Regular visits are one of the most powerful things you can do.
source_name: Judicial Council, The Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 10
source_says: The two most important steps to take to get your child back are to follow the case plan and visit your child.
steps: Opened the booklet PDF, read p. 10 and p. 24 ('it's very important to visit your child').

title: Visit Your Child Consistently
statement: The court tracks attendance carefully — missing visits without a good reason can count against you.
source_says: That the parent or legal guardian has consistently and regularly contacted and visited with the child.
steps: Searched public.law for WIC 366.21, opened it. (g)(1)(A) makes consistent visiting a finding the court looks at; (e)(5) lets the court set a section 366.26 hearing within 120 days in listed cases where 'the parent has failed to contact and visit the child'. The booklet p. 25 says to call the worker before a visit you must miss to explain why.

title: Visit Your Child Consistently
statement: Go to every visit. Your child needs to see you, and the court keeps track.
source_says: That the parent or legal guardian has consistently and regularly contacted and visited with the child.
steps: Opened public.law WIC 366.21, read (g)(1)(A).

title: Visit Your Child Consistently
statement: WIC §362.1 – Visitation is critical to reunification. Court evaluates visitation consistency at review hearings.
source_says: Visitation shall be as frequent as possible, consistent with the well-being of the child.
steps: Opened public.law WIC 362.1. It supports the first half ('In order to maintain ties between the parent or guardian and any siblings and the child'). It has no words about the court judging a parent's visiting record at review hearings. That is in WIC 366.21(g)(1)(A), which the entry does not cite.
fix: WIC 362.1: visits should be as frequent as possible. WIC 366.21: at review hearings the court looks at whether you visited your child regularly.

title: Right to a Hearing Before Placement Gets Stricter
statement: If the county wants to move your child to a more restrictive placement, such as out of your home or from a relative to a foster home, it must file a petition and you have the right to a hearing.
source_says: shall be made only after noticed hearing upon a supplemental petition.
steps: Searched public.law for WIC 387, opened it. (a) requires a noticed hearing on a supplemental petition; (d) 'the clerk of the juvenile court shall immediately set the same for hearing within 30 days'. Booklet p. 33: 'This happens if CPS believes the child needs a more restrictive placement.' Both citations match.

title: Right to a Hearing Before Placement Gets Stricter
statement: The county cannot move your child to a stricter placement without a hearing.
source_says: Take into and maintain temporary custody of, without a warrant, a child ... who has been declared a dependent child of the juvenile court under Section 300
steps: Opened public.law WIC 387: the final order needs a noticed hearing, but (e) allows 'An order for the detention of the child pending adjudication of the petition' after a detention hearing. Opened public.law WIC 306(a)(2): a social worker may take a dependent child into temporary custody without a warrant when the child 'is in immediate danger of physical or sexual abuse' or similar. Rule 5.565(d) applies the initial hearing rules to supplemental petitions. So in an emergency the child can be moved before the hearing on the petition.
fix: The county must file a petition and there must be a hearing before a judge orders a stricter placement. In an emergency, your child can be moved first and the hearing comes soon after.

title: Right to Keep Making School and Health Decisions
statement: Even when your child is removed, you keep the right to make decisions about school and health care and to go to your child's doctor visits, unless the judge limits those rights.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, What to do if your child is removed; WIC 361(a)(1)
source_says: You still have the right to make educational decisions on behalf of your child. ... You also retain your right to make health care decisions for your child
steps: Searched selfhelp.courts.ca.gov, opened the parents guide, read the rights section; it also says 'you have the right to attend doctor appointments'. Opened public.law WIC 361(a)(1): 'the court may limit the control to be exercised over the dependent child'.

title: Right to Keep Making School and Health Decisions
statement: The judge can limit your school decision rights if you do not respond to or attend school meetings.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, What to do if your child is removed
source_says: The court can limit your right to make educational decisions ... based on your failure to respond to and participate in school meetings
steps: Opened the self-help parents guide and read the education sentence.

title: Right to Keep Making School and Health Decisions
statement: You still decide about your child's school and doctor unless the judge says no.
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide, What to do if your child is removed
source_says: You also retain your right to make health care decisions for your child
steps: Opened the self-help parents guide.

title: Right to Keep Making School and Health Decisions
statement: California Courts Self-Help Guide for parents; WIC §361(a)
source_says: limits the right of the parent, guardian, or Indian custodian to make educational or developmental services decisions
steps: Opened public.law WIC 361, read (a)(1): 'The limitations may not exceed those necessary to protect the child.' Note: 361(a) covers school and developmental services decisions. It does not mention health care or school meetings; those come from the self-help guide, which the entry also cites.
